nameStory: The Wandering House Cobweaver gets its name from its tendency to move around inside homes rather than staying put in one web location like many house spiders. Unlike its stay-at-home cousin the Common House Spider, this species seems restless, often abandoning perfectly good webs to build new ones elsewhere. The 'cobweaver' part refers to its messy, irregular webs that look like the classic Halloween cobweb.
description: The Wandering House Cobweaver is a small, brownish spider that builds irregular cobwebs in the corners of buildings. Originally from tropical Asia, this introduced species has made itself at home in North American houses over the past few decades. It's quite small, typically less than half an inch including legs, with a rounded abdomen and relatively long, thin legs. You're most likely to spot one scurrying across a wall or hanging in a messy web near a window or ceiling corner.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds irregular, messy cobwebs with sticky capture threads hanging down - these feel tacky when you accidentally walk into them and cling to your face or hands

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Frequently abandons webs and builds new ones elsewhere, often moving locations every few days rather than maintaining one permanent web

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small rounded abdomen with a somewhat glossy appearance, attached to a smaller front section by a narrow waist

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length around 1/4 inch, with legs spanning roughly the size of a nickel when fully extended

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brownish coloration with subtle darker markings on the abdomen that may be difficult to see without close inspection

habitat: Found almost exclusively inside heated buildings in New England, particularly in basements, garages, and quiet corners of houses. Prefers areas near windows where flying insects might be trapped, and seems to favor spots with minimal human disturbance. As an introduced tropical species, it cannot survive New England winters outdoors and depends entirely on human structures for survival.

seasonality.spring: Active indoors year-round but may become more noticeable as they begin reproducing. Look for small egg sacs in web corners.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with frequent web-building and abandonment cycles. Most likely time to spot them moving between locations.
seasonality.fall: Continues indoor activity as outdoor spiders begin seeking winter shelter, but this species is already established inside. May produce late-season egg sacs.
seasonality.winter: Remains active in heated spaces while native spiders are dormant. This is actually a good time to spot them since there's less competition from other house spiders.

funFact: This spider is such a recent arrival to North America that it wasn't even scientifically described until 1980, making it younger than many of the people reading this - it's essentially a spider immigrant that's still in the process of spreading across the continent!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Common House Spider, but the Wandering House Cobweaver's restless behavior is the key difference - if you see the same spider web get abandoned and rebuilt somewhere else nearby within a few days, you're probably looking at a Wandering House Cobweaver rather than the more settled Common House Spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'house' spider, this is actually a very recent introduction to New England homes. Many field guides from before the 1990s won't include this species at all, which can be confusing for people using older identification resources.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Common House Spider, the Wandering House Cobweaver is slightly smaller and much more likely to abandon its web site. Both build similar irregular cobwebs, but the Common House Spider typically maintains the same web location for weeks or months, while the Wandering House Cobweaver moves frequently. The wandering behavior is really the most reliable way to tell them apart in the field.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Wandering House Cobweaver has similar web-building habits but tends to move its web location more frequently and has slightly different abdominal markings.
